A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same encoder-redundancy study. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison, including the rasterized plots.

before.justification: v2 reports original encoder-masking evaluations, CUR/IG measurements, attention analyses, and masking ablations in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v3 retains those original experiments and additionally reports training, latency, computational-cost, and trained-versus-masked results in Tables 17–20.

M1.justification: The proposed diagnostic procedure remains combinatorial encoder masking with CUR and IG. The zero-masking procedure and mean-masking alternative are retained. Training compact variants supplies additional experimental controls rather than a new proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: Appendix A and Table 5 retain the same 15 benchmarks and four task categories. The added model configurations and efficiency measurements introduce no identified dataset, domain, or task coverage; latency is measured on the existing MME benchmark.

E2.justification: Table 20 introduces separately trained compact Eagle variants as explicit comparators to post-hoc masking, and Figure 2 adds the DeepSeek-VL 1.3B configuration. DeepSeek-VL 7B was already evaluated in v2's Table 12. Newly discussed MOVE and Mixpert are not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: v3 adds a trained-versus-masked comparison design, a latency protocol averaging 2,374 MME samples with generation capped at one token, and compute profiling for a 64-token prompt and one-token answer. Figure 2 also adds a 1.3B model configuration. These substantially extend evaluation procedures; Appendix A's existing benchmark protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: Tables 17–20 add substantial efficiency analyses and test whether training with fewer encoders reproduces the performance obtained by masking a fully trained model. Per-encoder FLOPs further examine where computational costs arise. Existing attention, model-size, masking-operation, and case-study analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. Figure 2's minima, maxima, and means describe encoder subsets, not repeated experimental runs; the expanded plot retains this practice.

E6.justification: Most original table values remain unchanged, but v3 adds DeepSeek-VL 1.3B curves and Tables 17–20. New results include dual-encoder Eagle scores of 60.95 when trained versus 62.48 when masked, and full-versus-dual latency of 749.656 versus 603.153 ms. The reported training speedup changes from 1.69× to 1.53×, and the fine-tuning cost claim changes from 1700 to 94.57 A100 GPU hours; inconsistent time units prevent interpreting this as a comparable cost reduction.

T1.justification: The architecture formulation, CUR/IG definitions, and benchmark aggregation equation remain unchanged in Equations 1–4. The new Platonic Representation Hypothesis discussion is conceptual interpretation, without a new formal assumption, theorem, proof, or derivation.

C1.justification: The central redundancy and encoder-specialization claims remain. The abstract adds reduced inference latency, while the contributions and conclusion emphasize practical inefficiency and compact models' accuracy–cost trade-off more explicitly, replacing the earlier contribution focused on redundancy drivers and dynamic weighting.

C2.justification: v3 adds representational convergence as a mechanism explanation and interprets trained-versus-masked differences as possible benefits of additional encoders during training. Limitations are substantially rewritten around static fusion, dynamic routing, untested robustness/fairness dimensions, and post-hoc applicability. It adds specific ethical risks but removes v2's explicit warning that single-encoder CUR misses higher-order interactions.

D1.justification: v3 adds localized reproducibility details: single-node training on eight A100 GPUs, stage timings, encoder input resolutions, and timing/profiling settings. Table 20 refers to the official Eagle training recipe without reproducing its hyperparameters. A new statement promises code and model release upon acceptance but supplies no access location; Appendix C's explicit torch.mean note is removed.

R1.justification: New Section 2.3 positions the study relative to expert routing and token selection, adding MOVE and Mixpert citations. The discussion additionally cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. Existing related-work sections and references are otherwise retained, making this a focused expansion.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the contribution list, limitations, and conclusion; adds focused related-work, efficiency, discussion, ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use passages; and updates author information and headers. Most existing prose and the main section/appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is rebuilt from four panels into a nine-panel grid, largely redisplaying existing appendix results while adding DeepSeek-VL 1.3B. Four new efficiency/comparison tables are added, Table 3 incorporates existing DeepSeek-VL 7B results, and several displays move. Figures 1, 3, 4, and 5 retain their content.

improvement.justification: Tables 17–20 strengthen v2's sparsely supported efficiency argument through trained-versus-masked controls and measured latency, making the practical trade-off more assessable. The gain is limited by reporting problems: Section 4.2 claims over 96% retention for a trained variant whose Table 17 scores imply about 94%, and training totals and FLOPs accounting are internally inconsistent. Removing the higher-order CUR limitation also weakens qualification of the unchanged metric.
